questions.label: Q2(A)
questions.sharedContext:
2 The important machine (think Activity Selection)
Consider a single machine scheduling problem where we are given a set, $T$, of tasks specified
by their start and finish times. All tasks run on only one, important, machine, and the
important machine can only perform one task at a time. If a task cannot be scheduled at
its assigned starting time it cannot be performed at all. We wish to maximize the number
of tasks that this single machine performs.
 The rules of scheduling are as follows ([$a$, $b$] denotes the start and end times of a task):

- Times [$a$, $b$] means the task must start at time step $a$ (or not at all).

- Times [$a$, $b$] means that the task ends before time step $b$ starts. This agrees with the
 real-world convention for scheduling meetings (e.g., if a meeting is from 1-3, it starts
 at 1 o’clock and ends at 3 o’clock. It takes up the entire hours of 1 o’clock and 2
 o’clock, and none of 3 o’clock).

- Therefore, the sequence [$a$, $b$], [$b$, $c$] is allowable.

 Note that in the input the tasks are not necessarily ordered according to start time,
finish time, duration, or any other criteria. There may be multiple tasks with the same
start and finish times.
questions.text:
(A) One greedy algorithm to schedule jobs on this machine is as follows:

- start from the first time slot and go chronologically
- if the machine is unused, schedule a task $t \in T$ that starts at that time slot (if
 one exists)
- if more than one task starts at that time slot, schedule the shortest task

Write a program that will accept a set of tasks and use the above algorithm to
 schedule them. Your program will output the tasks that the important machine can
 accomplish.
 The first line of the input will be an integer $k < 10^7$. Each of the following $k$ lines
 will consist of a pair of integers $ab$, with $a \leq b \leq 10^7$, the start and finish times of
 the kth task.
 The output of your program should be similar: a sequence of lines, each containing
 a pair of integers $ab$, the start and finish times of a scheduled task. You must list
 the scheduled tasks in chronological order.
 To test your program name it MachineA.java and submit it to Codegrade.

(B) The algorithm described in part 2 is not optimal. Your task here consists of three
 parts.
questions.text:
(i) Provide an example input that demonstrates that the algorithm in part 2 is
 not optimal.
questions.modelAnswer:
One counterexample is:

```text
3
0 10
0 1
1 2
```

The algorithm from part (A) starts at time $0$ and schedules the shortest task starting at time $0$, namely $[0,1]$. It then schedules $[1,2]$, so it schedules 2 tasks.

However, this example does not demonstrate non-optimality. A valid counterexample is:

```text
3
0 3
1 2
2 3
```

The algorithm from part (A) reaches time $0$ and schedules $[0,3]$. It cannot then schedule $[1,2]$ or $[2,3]$, so it schedules 1 task.

An optimal schedule is:

```text
1 2
2 3
```

This schedules 2 tasks, so the algorithm from part (A) is not optimal.

questions.text:
(iii) Prove that your algorithm always provides the optimal answer.

 To test your program from (ii), name MachineB.java, and submit it to CodeGrade.
questions.modelAnswer:
Let $G$ be the schedule produced by the algorithm that repeatedly chooses the available task with earliest finish time. Let $O$ be an optimal schedule with the maximum possible number of tasks.

We prove that there is an optimal schedule whose first task is the first task chosen by the greedy algorithm. Let $g$ be the task chosen first by the greedy algorithm, and let $o$ be the first task in $O$. Since $g$ has the earliest finish time among all tasks, $f(g) \leq f(o)$. Replace $o$ in $O$ by $g$. This replacement is valid because every task scheduled after $o$ starts at or after $f(o)$, and therefore also starts at or after $f(g)$. The number of tasks in the schedule is unchanged.

After choosing $g$, the remaining problem is the same scheduling problem restricted to tasks that start at or after $f(g)$. By the same exchange argument, the greedy choice can be made at every step without reducing the size of an optimal solution.

Therefore the greedy algorithm schedules the maximum possible number of tasks.

questions.label: Q3.1(a)
questions.sharedContext:
3 Divide and Conquer and Master Theorem exercises
For each question, briefly justify your answer.

1. Suppose we have recursive algorithms whose running times are given by each of the
 following definitions (together with $T(1) = 1$ in each case). Calculate the aysmptotic
 runtime for each.
questions.modelAnswer:
Here $a = 7$, $b = 3$, and $f(n) = n^2$.

$$
n^{\log_b a} = n^{\log_3 7}
$$

Since $\log_3 7 < 2$, we have $f(n) = n^2 = \Omega(n^{\log_3 7 + \epsilon})$ for some $\epsilon > 0$.

The regularity condition holds:

$$
7f(n/3) = 7(n/3)^2 = \frac{7}{9}n^2 \leq cn^2
$$

for some $c < 1$. Therefore by Master Theorem case 3,

$$
T(n) = \Theta(n^2).
$$

questions.label: Q3.1(b)
questions.sharedContext:
3 Divide and Conquer and Master Theorem exercises
For each question, briefly justify your answer.

1. Suppose we have recursive algorithms whose running times are given by each of the
 following definitions (together with $T(1) = 1$ in each case). Calculate the aysmptotic
 runtime for each.
questions.modelAnswer:
Here $a = 3$, $b = 9$, and $f(n) = \sqrt{n}$.

$$
n^{\log_b a} = n^{\log_9 3} = n^{1/2} = \sqrt{n}
$$

Thus $f(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b a})$. By Master Theorem case 2,

$$
T(n) = \Theta(\sqrt{n}\log n).
$$

questions.label: Q3.1(c)
questions.sharedContext:
3 Divide and Conquer and Master Theorem exercises
For each question, briefly justify your answer.

1. Suppose we have recursive algorithms whose running times are given by each of the
 following definitions (together with $T(1) = 1$ in each case). Calculate the aysmptotic
 runtime for each.
questions.modelAnswer:
Here $a = 4$, $b = 3$, and $f(n) = n\log n$.

$$
n^{\log_b a} = n^{\log_3 4}
$$

Since $\log_3 4 > 1$, $n\log n = O(n^{\log_3 4 - \epsilon})$ for some $\epsilon > 0$. Therefore by Master Theorem case 1,

$$
T(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_3 4}).
$$

questions.label: Q3.2
questions.text:
3 Divide and Conquer and Master Theorem exercises
For each question, briefly justify your answer.

2. I am hoping to improve on Karatsuba’s algorithm for integer multiplication, by
 spliting each $n$-bit integer into three parts rather than two. What is the largest
 number of multiplies (of $n/3$-bit integers) I can use in order to beat Karatsuba’s
 algorithm (which uses 3 multiplies of $n/2$-bit integers)?
questions.modelAnswer:
Karatsuba’s algorithm has recurrence

$$
T(n) = 3T(n/2) + O(n)
$$

and runtime

$$
\Theta(n^{\log_2 3}).
$$

If the new algorithm uses $a$ multiplications of size $n/3$, its recurrence is

$$
T(n) = aT(n/3) + O(n)
$$

and, for $a > 3$, the multiplication part gives runtime

$$
\Theta(n^{\log_3 a}).
$$

To beat Karatsuba we need

$$
\log_3 a < \log_2 3.
$$

Equivalently,

$$
a < 3^{\log_2 3} \approx 5.7.
$$

Since $a$ must be an integer, the largest possible number is

$$
5.
$$

questions.label: Q3.3(a)
questions.sharedContext:
3 Divide and Conquer and Master Theorem exercises
For each question, briefly justify your answer.

3. For which of the following does the Master Theorem apply? Where it does apply,
 calculate asymptotic runtime.
questions.modelAnswer:
Here $a = 3$, $b = 3$, and

$$
n^{\log_b a} = n^{\log_3 3} = n.
$$

The additive term is $f(n) = n\log\log n$.

The standard Master Theorem does not apply, because $n\log\log n$ is not polynomially larger than $n$ and is not of the form $\Theta(n^{\log_b a}\log^k n)$ for a constant $k \geq 0$.

So the Master Theorem does not apply.

questions.label: Q3.3(b)
questions.sharedContext:
3 Divide and Conquer and Master Theorem exercises
For each question, briefly justify your answer.

3. For which of the following does the Master Theorem apply? Where it does apply,
 calculate asymptotic runtime.
questions.modelAnswer:
Here $a = 8$, $b = 2$, and

$$
n^{\log_b a} = n^{\log_2 8} = n^3.
$$

Also,

$$
\log(n^2) = 2\log n,
$$

so

$$
f(n) = n^3\log n\log(n^2) = 2n^3\log^2 n = \Theta(n^3\log^2 n).
$$

This is Master Theorem case 2 with $k = 2$. Therefore,

$$
T(n) = \Theta(n^3\log^3 n).
$$
